name: Ben Young

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government, and we don't sell anything or campaign for any side. Your answers are confidential. What does a normal working day look like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I get on the building site before seven and carry timber, cut battens, and clear up behind the carpenters. I'm 58 and still learning bits of the trade; my pay is low, but I like seeing a wall stand straight by Friday. My knees are sore by the bus ride home, and there's hardly another site hiring near us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the lads there's always a machine coming to save us time, and most of us still have to lift the boards. The foreman can have his little scheduling program if it keeps the timber arriving on time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truth is, I'm already counting days between pay packets. My partner Joan works a few shifts at the bakery, and we have less than a month's bills put by.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep taking the early bus and ask the foreman for the next site when this one ends. In the first year I'd drop our Friday takeaway and put that money against the electricity arrears.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm uneasy even with AI doing very little. A dry spell between jobs would hurt us faster than any new software.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Joan after a short week?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my partner Joan exactly what came in, rather than pretend Friday's pay was normal. Our grown children have rent of their own, so I won't make them our emergency fund.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You sound worried even in the mild picture; what keeps you at this site?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The foreman knows I turn up and I'm willing to sweep as well as cut. Starting somewhere new at 58 with no certificate is a gamble I can't pay for.

say: I'd say **site work** still needs hands to carry timber and make cuts.
I'd tell the crew a better **delivery schedule** might spare us a wasted morning.
think: I know our **thin savings** leave no room for a gap between sites.
I worry my **sore knees** could cost more work than this mild AI change.
do: Keep taking the **early bus** to the current building site.
Ask the foreman about the **next site** before this one finishes.
Drop Friday **takeaway** and pay the electricity arrears.
feel: **Uneasy** about money even if AI stays small.
S0.quote: Our grown children have rent of their own, so I won't make them our emergency fund.
fieldNote: He describes a familiar site routine but repeatedly returns to **short weeks** and the gap between contracts.
He treats the foreman's trust as an asset because few employers nearby would take a **junior worker** of his age.

steps.text: Keep taking the early bus to the current building site
Ask the foreman for work on the next site
Drop Friday takeaway and pay electricity arrears

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the office people will feel it before the ones carrying plasterboard. I'd ask the foreman whether fewer orders on his screen means fewer shifts for us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't know who'll still pay for new rooms if other people lose their work. Even if a robot is slow to arrive, a quiet building site can send me home on Thursday.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the job while there's timber to fit and check the noticeboard each week for labouring work. In the first year of the change I'd take a Saturday clearing job if the foreman has one and stop replacing my old phone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This makes me anxious because a lost day is real money in our kitchen. I can still walk onto a site, but there aren't many around here.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would one lost day mean at home?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Joan would cover groceries from her bakery shifts, and I'd delay the heating payment a week. I hate saying that aloud, but the sums don't bend.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you try the software that orders timber?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I never use AI tools, and I wouldn't touch an order without someone checking it. If the foreman shows me a simple screen, I might watch, but I won't bet a wage on it.

say: I'd say **office tasks** will change before carrying boards does.
I'd ask whether slower **orders** mean fewer site shifts.
think: I fear lost income elsewhere could leave our **building site** quiet.
I know even one missed **shift** would push a household bill back.
do: Keep fitting **timber** while the foreman has site work.
Check the site **noticeboard** weekly for labouring shifts.
Take a **Saturday clearing job** if the foreman offers one.
feel: **Anxious** about hours disappearing before robots arrive.
S1.quote: Even if a robot is slow to arrive, a quiet building site can send me home on Thursday.
fieldNote: His public distinction between office work and site work gives way to a fear about **customer demand**.
He will watch a tool demonstration, but his actual first response is to seek **extra shifts** and preserve cash.

steps.text: Check site noticeboard weekly for labouring shifts
Take a Saturday clearing job if the foreman offers one
Stop replacing the old phone this year

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew the thinking machine won't carry a door up the stairs in 2028. I'd still ask the foreman if there's a site booked after this one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 60, I might get three more years of fitting and clearing after the thinking work goes. Around 2031, when robots can do that work too, a junior like me may be the first told not to come back.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Starting now I'd ask the foreman for written dates on this job and keep a paper list of local maintenance firms. In the first year after 2028 I'd apply for caretaker work at the school and bank any extra site days toward our rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm alarmed by how little time that leaves. I don't have a course fee saved or another trade to pull out of my pocket.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Joan about 2031?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my partner Joan that the robot date is the real cliff for my wages. We'd look at the rent together, not tell the children they're expected to take us in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the school has no caretaker opening?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the housing association about cleaning and small repairs, then take whatever paid site days remain. I can't retire at 61 just because a machine starts carrying boards.

say: I'd say **2028 AI** will change office planning before it changes my hands-on work.
I'd ask the foreman for the **next contract** rather than make promises to the crew.
think: I expect **robots around 2031** could remove the junior site work that pays our rent.
I know a new trade course is hard with **no spare money** and little time.
do: Ask the foreman for **written dates** on the present job.
Apply for **school caretaker work** in the year after 2028.
Bank any extra **site days** toward rent while construction work remains.
feel: **Alarmed** that the likely loss comes before retirement is affordable.
S2.quote: I can't retire at 61 just because a machine starts carrying boards.
fieldNote: He marks a sharp difference between the thinking AI date and the **2031 robot date** for his manual work.
His plan depends on continued paid work; he has neither a funded course nor a **retirement cushion**.

steps.text: Ask foreman for written dates on the current site
Apply for school caretaker work after 2028
Ask housing association about cleaning and small repairs if school has no opening
Bank pay from extra site days toward future rent

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years gives a working crew time to see which jobs actually vanish. I'd want the foreman to show us the next contracts, not just a clever video.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll be 63 when thinking AI arrives in 2031 and 66 when capable robots turn up around 2034. The three years before robots arrive could carry me nearer stopping, but we still won't have enough saved to stop on a date in a brochure.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay on this site and ask to shadow the caretaker at the community hall one afternoon a month if he agrees. In the first year after 2031 I'd apply for paid building maintenance posts, while still taking site shifts until a real offer comes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm anxious, though less cornered than with 2028. Five years would let me knock on doors before my wages disappear.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why the community hall?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I fixed a loose rail there after a weekend event, and the caretaker said there are always small jobs. I can already handle a hammer, though I'd need someone to teach me the heating checks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you pay for that training yourself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, not from less than one month's savings. If the hall offered paid training, I'd take it, but I won't borrow to chase a promise.

say: I'd say the **five-year warning** lets us watch real site contracts.
I'd ask for work dates instead of accepting a **sales video** as proof.
think: I may reach **66** before site robots arrive, yet still need wages then.
I could move into **building maintenance** if someone teaches the checks on paid time.
do: Ask to shadow the **community hall caretaker** monthly if he agrees.
Apply for paid **maintenance posts** in the year after 2031.
Continue taking **site shifts** until another employer offers wages.
feel: **Anxious**, but able to make calls before the work goes.
S3.quote: The three years before robots arrive could carry me nearer stopping, but we still won't have enough saved to stop on a date in a brochure.
fieldNote: He does not equate reaching retirement age with the money to **leave paid work**.
His modest change of course is grounded in a past repair at the hall and a possible **paid introduction**.

steps.text: Ask to shadow community hall caretaker monthly if he agrees
Apply for paid building maintenance posts after 2031
Take paid heating-check training if the hall offers it
Continue taking site shifts until another paid offer comes

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew I might be an old man by the time the carrying robots arrive. That doesn't make the ten years free; we still need work each month until then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 68 in 2036, I would be 71 when robots arrive around 2039. I'd like to stop climbing stairs by then, but with our thin savings I can't promise that either of us can retire.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working now and ask the hall caretaker about a paid helper shift this winter. In the first year after 2036 I'd take ground-floor repair jobs if my knees allow, and apply for a porter post if the site hours dry up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel some relief at having a decade, with a nagging fear about my body. The machine might beat my knees to the finish, or my knees might go first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you and Joan change this year?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd pay down the electricity arrears and keep the old sofa another year. I won't tell my partner Joan we have a retirement plan when we have only a few weeks of bills saved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would your children help with the longer runway?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask our grown children for a lift to an interview, not their rent money. They have their own households, and I'd rather keep a paid job I can manage.

say: I'd say the **robot date** comes when I may already be too old for heavy carrying.
I'd remind the crew that **monthly wages** matter throughout the decade.
think: I want to stop climbing stairs, but **thin savings** may keep me employed past 70.
I fear my **knees** could fail before the work does.
do: Ask the hall caretaker for a **paid helper shift** this winter.
Take **ground-floor repairs** after 2036 if my knees allow.
Apply for a **porter post** if site hours dry up.
feel: **Relieved** by the extra time, yet worried about physical wear.
S4.quote: The machine might beat my knees to the finish, or my knees might go first.
fieldNote: The longer horizon changes his timing more than his appetite for risk; he still needs **paid work**.
He limits future tasks by what his knees can do and rejects relying on his **grown children** for bills.

steps.text: Ask community hall caretaker for a paid helper shift this winter
Take ground-floor repair work after 2036 if knees allow
Apply for a porter post if site hours dry up

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because I could lose the site wage by 2031 with no savings to bridge it. A written run of work and a paid route into maintenance would help more than a speech about learning new things.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask how long a person can still lift boards every morning. My knees are part of the money question, even if no robot ever arrives.

headlineQuote: My knees are part of the money question, even if no robot ever arrives.
portrait: Ben is a **58-year-old junior** construction worker who likes tangible work but has sore knees and low pay.
He and his partner have **less than a month** of expenses saved, with few nearby sites hiring.
He resists new tools and seeks **paid maintenance work** as the robot dates approach.
Even in the decade-long scenario, he expects to **keep earning** rather than count on retirement.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** leaves Ben exposed to a possible site wage loss by 2031.
whatWouldHelp: A **written work schedule** and a paid route into maintenance would help him prepare.
